 Daylight saving time is spooky this year: What to know about the 2026 clock change
 We’ll be getting an extra hour of shut-eye soon, but some say it actually may do more harm than good.
 SHARE Facebook LinkedIn Bluesky X Link ADD ON GOOGLE October 28, 2026 [Source photos: Adobe Stock]
 BY  Jennifer Mattson 
 Listen to this Article More info 0:00 / 0:00 It’s that time of year again—when the sun sets earlier, the days get shorter, and the nights get colder as we say goodbye to daylight saving time (DST).
 DST ends this weekend, in the early morning hours after Halloween for most of the U.S.
 If you are one of the many people who find the time change confusing, remember the clock “falls back” and a majority of the U.S. “gains” one more hour of sleep each autumn.
 Here’s what else to know.
 Subscribe to the Daily newsletter. Fast Company's trending stories delivered to you every day SIGN UP Privacy Policy |
 Fast Company Newsletters When exactly does daylight saving time end in 2026?
 This Sunday, November 1, at 2 a.m. local time, we’ll turn back the clocks to 1 a.m., saying goodbye to daylight saving time until March 14, 2027 .
 So we’ll get an extra hour of sleep?
 Yes—but although getting an extra hour of shut-eye sounds good, according to a growing consensus of health care providers, it actually may do more harm than good.
 While the majority of Americans (56%) favor making daylight saving permanent, a growing chorus of scientists and doctors disagree—including those from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Stanford Medicine . These health care professionals argue that sticking to permanent standard time is healthier because it doesn’t disrupt the body’s natural circadian rhythm, which can lead to all sorts of health problems, including higher rates of stroke and obesity.
